4.0.s.en: (1) The agreement of Deborah and Barak

4.0.0.en: The end of the previous chapter told us about another judge, Shamgar the son of Anath, but at the beginning of this chapter it returns to tell us about Ehud the son of Gera, mentioned before Shamgar. The explanation of this is that both judges were contemporaries, each judging a certain region other than the region of the other, and that Shamgar died before Ehud. So after the death of Ehud the children of Israel returned to their evils, as was their habit after the death of the judge.

4.1.0.en: The Lord sold them: the Lord delivered them into the hand of their enemies.

4.1.1.en: Harosheth of the Gentiles: a mixture of nations, and the town was so called because many nations lived in it (Map 11). The Lord delivered them into the hand of another pagan king, Jabin king of the Canaanites, who dwelt in the capital of his kingdom, Hazor, in the north of Palestine (Joshua had captured it, but the Canaanites returned and recovered it). This Jabin is not the King Jabin who lived in the days of Joshua (Josh 11). The commander of his army, "Sisera", was encamped with his soldiers in the city of "Harosheth of the Gentiles."

4.2.0.en: This king was cruel and merciless, and he treated the children of Israel with violence and harshness for twenty years, and his army was equipped with nine hundred chariots of iron, which frightened the children of Israel from making any attempt to stand against him. Perhaps Sisera was taking revenge for the first defeat of the Canaanites at the hand of Joshua (Josh 11).

4.3.0.en: Deborah: the meaning of her name is bee, and indeed she was active like a bee.

4.3.1.en: The judge of the people at that time was a prophetess, and she was the wife of a man named Lapidoth. Her being a prophetess means that she received spiritual messages from God with which she taught the people, in addition to her knowledge of the Law and her judging the people by it.

4.4.0.en: Ramah: the intended city is Ramah, belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, which is 8 km from Jerusalem. Bethel: it lies halfway between Jerusalem and Nablus (Map 11). Came up: Deborah used to sit in a high place, so they would go up to her.

4.4.1.en: Deborah the judge lived in a house under a palm tree named after her, and she used to sit outside it to receive those of the people who came to her so that she might judge between them. The location of her dwelling was in the mountainous land that was the portion of the tribe of Ephraim in the middle of Palestine. The palm tree and the house were in this land which lies between Ramah and Bethel.

4.4.2.en: The palm tree under which the prophetess Deborah sat to judge was called the palm tree of Deborah, in perpetuation of her memory. So also we name churches after the saints in remembrance of their lives, their faith and their service to the Lord.

4.5.0.en: Kedesh-naphtali: there are many cities named Kedesh, and this Kedesh lies in the tribe of Naphtali (Map 12). Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded: that is, the Lord commanded...

4.5.1.en: Go toward: advance quietly and slowly, then attack the Canaanites.

4.5.2.en: Mount Tabor: it is now Jebel et-Tur and lies about 9 km southeast of Nazareth.

4.5.3.en: Of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun: the two tribes were neighbors and near the city of Hazor in which the king of Canaan lived, so it was easy for them to gather for war.

4.5.4.en: God sent a message to the prophetess Deborah to summon a man named "Barak the son of Abinoam" from the city of Kedesh, and she informed him that the Lord had commanded him to go toward Mount Tabor and to take with him ten thousand men (because the Lord knows that the war requires this number). And He specified the two tribes from which he was to draw this number, the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun, because the portions of the two tribes lie near the center of residence of their enemies.

4.6.0.en: The river Kishon: a river that springs from Mount Tabor, passes through the plain of Acre and empties near Haifa, and on its bank Elijah the prophet killed the priests of Baal (1 Kgs 18:40). I will draw unto thee: God allows Sisera to rush forward to attack the children of Israel, so Barak defeats him and many of them are drowned in the river Kishon.

4.6.1.en: The Lord prompts Sisera to move with his armies toward the army of Barak to face him and fight him, so he heads to the broad place where the river Kishon flows, and the Lord breaks Sisera and many of his soldiers are drowned in the river, and Barak defeats him.

4.7.0.en: Barak insisted that the prophetess Deborah accompany him in his battle, for he esteems her spiritual standing and with her accompanying him he trusts that God will help him, and also that she may advise him of the things he should do as he fights Sisera, and also so that his men may be encouraged by her presence among them.

4.8.0.en: Deborah informed him of her readiness to go with him to encourage him, but she told him that her accompanying him deprives him of the full glory of the victory, which may be ascribed to her. At the same time she prophesied that the one who would decide the battle (by killing Sisera) would be a woman, Jael, as will come in (v. 21). Barak did not mind to whom the glory would go, and Deborah did not mind the hardship of the journey, so she went out to accompany him in the battle.

4.8.1.en: God rejoiced in the cooperation of Deborah and Barak. How beautiful it is to cooperate with those around you to achieve the needed success, and not to mind if the glory is ascribed to you, but rather to wish that it be ascribed to others, so that you keep your humility and the devil does not fight you with praise.

4.9.0.en: Barak called both tribes, Zebulun and Naphtali, for he himself was of the tribe of Naphtali, while Zebulun was the tribe neighboring it in the land. So the men of war came to him from the two tribes, and their number was ten thousand as the Lord had commanded him, and they all went up to Mount Tabor, next to the city of Kedesh in Galilee, and the prophetess Deborah accompanied them, whose going up with them was a strong factor in raising their morale and encouraging them.

4.9.1.en: Deborah went up with them. How great is the lesson we take from the conduct of this woman of great heart, for she did not carry within her a spirit of pride and domination but a spirit of love and gentleness; she did not issue commands with grandeur and arrogance but took part with support and encouragement; she did not plead her womanhood, and perhaps her advanced age, but went before the men, filling them with enthusiasm, strength and blessing.

4.10.0.en: Heber the Kenite: he was of the children of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses.

4.10.1.en: The children of Hobab: a part of the Kenites.

4.10.3.en: We learned earlier in (ch. 1:16) that the Kenites pitched their tents in the wilderness of Judah. And here the inspired writer mentions that Heber the Kenite separated from them, perhaps because of the scarcity of pasture and the fewness of springs of water, and went with his tents until he reached the oak trees in one of the outskirts of Zaanaim in the middle of Naphtali by the city of Kedesh. The place where Heber settled was near the battlefield where the fight between Barak and Sisera would take place.

4.11.0.en: Mount Tabor: a mountain in the land of Galilee.

4.11.1.en: The reconnaissance carried out by Sisera's men, whom he had spread throughout the land to report to him what was happening, brought word that Barak had gone up with his army to Mount Tabor in preparation for war.

4.12.0.en: Harosheth of the Gentiles: a town in the north of Palestine inhabited by a mixture of nations (Map 11). Sisera gathered his chariots and mustered an army from the region in which he was encamped, which lies between Harosheth of the Gentiles and the river Kishon, and prepared with them to fight the children of Israel under the leadership of Deborah and Barak.

4.13.0.en: Is not the Lord gone out before thee: it means that the Lord is going before you, leading your armies and achieving victory for you.

4.13.1.en: Deborah said to Barak, Up, and go down to meet Sisera, giving him the good news that God would deliver the Canaanites into his hand and he would defeat them on this day, assuring him that the Lord was going before him, leading his armies. Barak believed God's promise, so he did what Deborah called him to do and went down from Mount Tabor with his ten thousand men.

4.13.2.en: The Lord fulfilled His promise to Barak, spoken by the prophetess Deborah, that he would defeat Sisera. May we cling to the Lord's true promises and believe with complete faith everything He promised His beloved ones, He who said "I will not leave you comfortless", "Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world", "I will never leave you nor forsake you", "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world", Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

4.13.3.en: Let us take these promises as provision for the road, walking in it with assurance of the Lord's presence with us at all times, upholding our steps and raising us from our stumblings and leading us to a happy eternal life.

4.14.0.en: Here divine providence intervened, and Sisera was thrown into confusion and was troubled by the strength and courage of Barak and his men, who plied their swords among Sisera's soldiers and killed many of them. Sisera's fear increased, so he got down from his chariot to avoid being recognized by Barak and his soldiers and in order to be able to flee faster than he could if he stayed in his chariot, and to be able to hide behind the mountains or in the forests among the trees.

4.15.0.en: Sisera's army drew back and fled before Barak and his army, and Barak followed them and pursued them to Harosheth of the Gentiles, where their main camp and the headquarters of their commander Sisera were, and they were all killed by the sword of Barak and his men, and not one of them was left alive.

4.16.0.en: Sisera, in the state of terror and confusion that had seized him, decided to flee to the tents of Heber the Kenite that were near the battlefield, and took refuge in the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber, thinking that he would be safe, for it would not occur to his pursuers that he had taken refuge with a woman.

4.16.1.en: Jael was in the tent alone, perhaps because her husband was busy with his work, and it was the right of a woman to receive as a guest one who was in distress so as to rescue him and help him.

4.17.0.en: Jael heard someone running toward her tent, so she went out and saw that it was Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army, between whom and the clan of her husband there was peace. She welcomed him to receive him in her tent, and he went in to her, very tired from running in addition to his severe psychological exhaustion because of his defeat, so she arranged a place for him to sleep and covered him with a mantle so that he could rest and sleep.

4.18.0.en: A bottle of milk: the bottle is a skin bag in which milk is placed and ferments, which helped Sisera to fall into a deep sleep when he drank it.

4.18.1.en: He asked her to give him water to drink, so she opened the skin of milk and he drank from it, and when he had finished she covered him again with the mantle.

4.19.0.en: After Sisera felt secure with Jael, and this was by God's arrangement, he asked her to stand at the door of the tent, so that if she saw one of his pursuers and he asked her whether there was a man with her, she would answer no, and he would be ashamed to go in to search the tent because she was alone in it. This shows that he was still anxious and afraid that his enemies would overtake him.

4.20.0.en: A nail: a wooden stake pointed at its end, fixed in the ground and used to tie the ropes of the tent when it is pitched.

4.20.1.en: A hammer: a hand tool resembling a mallet, used to drive the nail into the ground.

4.20.2.en: Went softly unto him: walked toward him quietly.

4.20.4.en: While Sisera was deep in his sleep, Jael took the pointed tent nail in one hand and the hammer in the other and walked quietly toward Sisera, and she placed the nail on Sisera's temple and struck it with the hammer, and it pierced Sisera's head until it reached the ground and fastened his head to the ground, and because he was deep in sleep he did not wake to resist her, and he died.

4.20.5.en: Although the clan of the Kenites was at peace with Jabin king of Canaan, Jael and her husband were at the same time on strong terms with the children of Israel, for they lived next to the tribe of Judah. And Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses, was of the Kenites, so there was a strong tie and love between the people of God and the Kenites. When the Kenites saw the injustice and enslavement of the children of Israel by Jabin for many years, they were troubled by him and sympathized with their Jewish brethren, and this sympathy increased in the heart of Jael by the grace of God, so she became opposed to the injustice of the Canaanites, whom Sisera, the commander of their armies, represented, and her faith in the goodness of the children of Israel increased when God strengthened His people and they defeated Sisera, so she moved to help them and to kill the commander of the unjust enemy armies.

4.20.6.en: Do not exalt yourself or boast of your strength, however great, because it is God who gave it to you, and do not wrong others lest God take away your strength and humble you before others until you repent and return to Him. For God gave you your gifts and abilities so that you might thank Him and glorify Him and use them to bring happiness to those around you.

4.20.7.en: The song of Deborah and Barak

5.0.0.en: The Lord had delivered His people from the tyranny of the Chaldeans and their king Jabin by the hands of Deborah and Barak. So the two set out praising the Lord and singing the song of victory. This reminds us of the singing of Miriam, the sister of Aaron, after the deliverance from the slavery of the Egyptians. Thanking God is a necessary thing for the spiritual person, but sadly many ask, and after they obtain what they ask for, neglect thanksgiving.

5.1.0.en: For that the leaders took the lead: glorify the Lord for raising up leaders who achieved deliverance for the people. For that the people offered themselves willingly: glorify the Lord who called thousands to fight for His people, and they answered His call. Deborah calls her people to glorify God for two things:

5.1.1.en: 1- The commanders of the army by whom the victory was won under the leadership of Barak.

5.1.2.en: 2- The soldiers of the children of Israel who fought and conquered.

5.1.3.en: And we learn here to encourage everyone, for Deborah encourages the commanders and the soldiers and does not ascribe the glory to herself.

5.2.0.en: A call to the kings and great men of the pagan peoples, who often showed hostility and stirred up wars against the people of God, to look and know how God gives victory to His people.

5.2.1.en: I am Deborah, and the Lord brought about that great victory by my hand, therefore I sing to Him, rejoicing in the victory and in His great work with me and with my people. I do not sing with the tongue only, but with the pipe and instruments of music, as an expression of my great joy at the victory.

5.3.0.en: Seir: the land of Edom, the descendants of Esau, which lies in the northeast of the wilderness of Sinai.

5.3.2.en: The heavens dropped: rain came down from heaven.

5.3.3.en: Deborah reminds the people of God's former dealings with them when they crossed the wilderness at their exodus from Egypt, and how the Lord went out with His people to go around Edom (which is sometimes called the land of Seir) by a hard and wearisome road after the Edomites refused to let the people pass through their land (Num 20:22, 21:4). The matter of the earth trembling when the people passed was not mentioned before, but tradition preserved it until Deborah mentioned it in her song. The trembling of the earth was accompanied by the coming down of rain, and these phenomena took place by the Lord's arrangement as a declaration of His glory and a condemnation of the Edomites' defiance of His people.

5.4.0.en: Deborah also reminds them of what happened on the day the Law was given on Mount Sinai, when the mountains quaked at the awe and majesty of the glory of the Lord who was manifested on the mountain. This was mentioned in (Ex 19:18).

5.4.1.en: Thanking God and glorifying Him for His gifts to you gladdens your heart, confirms your faith in Him and drives you with enthusiasm to bear the various difficulties and responsibilities, so that you enjoy a surpassing divine work in you.

5.5.s.en: (2) The judges rescue the people from humiliation

5.5.0.en: Shamgar the son of Anath: one of the judges of the children of Israel, a contemporary of Deborah and Barak, who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with a long staff like that used to prick an animal if it lagged in its walking.

5.5.1.en: The highways were unoccupied: the roads became empty.

5.5.2.en: By-ways: side roads that were not paved.

5.5.3.en: Because the enemies occupied the lands of the children of Israel in the days of Shamgar and Jael, chaos and thieves spread, and the main paved roads were full of highwaymen, and instead of traveling on them, travelers were forced to walk on unpaved roads to avoid falling into the hands of highwaymen, which lengthened the time of travel, besides the hardship and weariness the travelers suffered.

5.6.0.en: The rulers of Israel were unable to deliver their people from the oppression of the enemies and their humiliation of the children of Israel until the Lord raised me up and urged me to work to rescue my people. And Deborah's leadership of the people was not domination but care and motherhood toward her people, so she was like a spiritual mother to them.

5.7.0.en: They chose new gods: the people forsook their true God and chose to worship new gods, newly invented and strange, which their fathers had not known before.

5.7.1.en: Then was war in the gates: the enemies attacked the gates of the children of Israel.

5.7.2.en: A shield: a piece of wood covered with leather which the warrior carries to protect himself from arrows.

5.7.3.en: All the disgrace and humiliation that came upon the people was caused by their forsaking the worship of the living God and choosing new, strange gods which their fathers had not known. And the result of their betrayal of the Lord was that He forsook them and allowed their enemies to lie in wait for them at the gates of their cities and besiege them, so as not to let them pass through them.

5.7.4.en: And among the signs of the humiliation of the people of God by their enemies was that they forbade them to bear arms, by taking their weapons from them, so none of the men able to fight had military equipment such as shields and spears, and his saying forty thousand is an estimated number for the people in this region.

5.8.0.en: My heart's love and my thanks I direct to the judges of Israel whom God chose from the people, who accepted the task they were assigned and rose to work in the midst of difficult circumstances. And we, the people of the Lord, must thank Him and glorify Him because it is He who prepared these leaders for us and strengthened them with His help and support.

5.9.0.en: She asses: the plural of she-ass, the female donkey.

5.9.1.en: Ashen (al-sahr): the plural of "ashar", a dusty color or a red tinged with white.

5.9.2.en: Rugs (al-tanafis): the plural of "tinfisa", a precious rug.

5.9.3.en: Deborah calls the rich, whom she symbolized as those who ride on red asses (a rare kind of donkey that none but the rich can afford to own), and whom she also symbolized as those who sit on precious carpets; she called them and the poor alike, who walk on their feet to move from place to place because they do not own she-asses to ride, she called everyone to praise the Lord and glorify Him.

5.9.4.en: The leader has importance in achieving success and joining people to God. So be faithful in bearing your responsibilities toward those around you and guiding them in the way of God.

5.10.0.en: Those who divide the spoil between the watering troughs: those who divide the spoils into portions and bring them to the water troughs to drink.

5.10.1.en: The people of the Lord went down to the gates: after the victory was achieved, the people were able to return to sit at the gates of the city for judgment, recreation or counsel.

5.10.2.en: She also calls those who divide the spoils of war into portions after their victory under the leadership of the judges, each one taking his portion and bringing it to the water troughs to drink. The animals were an important part of the spoils of war. These sing at the troughs, glorifying the Lord for His justice in vindicating His people and vindicating their rulers and restoring their rights seized from the hand of their enemies. For after the great victory the Lord granted to His people, the people were able to sit at the gates of the city as they used to before, for counsel and conversation, and to go out and come in through them with a freedom of which they had been deprived during the enemies' siege. And by this security prevailed and the chaos and injustice that were in the days of the occupation came to an end.

5.11.0.en: Deborah addresses herself saying: Rise up and awake to sing the song of victory, for the time of sorrow has passed and the time of joy has come. Then she addresses Barak saying: Arise to take the captives and the spoils from the enemy over whom the Lord gave you victory.

5.12.0.en: The one that remaineth (the fugitive): the one of the children of Israel who fled in the days of the occupation.

5.12.1.en: The fugitive had dominion over the nobles of the people: the children of Israel who were formerly fleeing before their enemies today have dominion over them and over their great men.

5.12.2.en: The children of Israel who were formerly fleeing before their enemies have today become their masters and have dominion over them and over the great men of the Canaanite people.

5.12.3.en: Then Deborah recalls the great work of the Lord with her and with Barak, who sings with her the same song, in that the Lord gave them authority over the mighty enemies.

5.13.s.en: (3) Praise of the tribes that took part in the war

5.13.0.en: Out of Ephraim: from the tribe of Ephraim, which includes large numbers of soldiers.

5.13.1.en: Whose root was against Amalek (their dwelling among Amalek): their dwelling among the Amalekites, who are among the oldest peoples of the region.

5.13.2.en: Benjamin: the intended tribe is Benjamin, one of the tribes of Israel. Although their number was small, they were strong.

5.13.3.en: Machir: the son of Manasseh (that is, the grandson of Joseph), from whom came army commanders, and they dwelt west of the Jordan. They that handle the pen of the writer (holding the commander's staff): bearers of the commander's scepter, which indicates their leadership of the army, and they used to count the soldiers.

5.13.4.en: From this verse to (v. 18) Deborah praises some of the tribes of the children of Israel who answered the call and took part in the war against the Canaanites, and she blames some other tribes that were slack about the war and the tribes dwelling far from the field of war for their negligence.

5.13.5.en: She begins with the tribe of Ephraim, who hastened to go out to the war despite the danger of leaving their land, which was surrounded by the Amalekites. And the tribe of Benjamin followed it to join the ranks of the fighters. Then she praises the descendants of Machir the son of Manasseh, who also went out to the war with their chiefs. And it is mentioned that the tribe of Zebulun had the leading position in making the plans and moving the army, and Barak had called the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali to take part with him in the war and gave it the leadership (ch. 4:10).

5.14.0.en: The divisions: branches of the Jordan River that run in the land of Reuben.

5.14.1.en: Great thoughts of heart (great searchings of heart): many discussions and consultations.

5.14.2.en: The princes of Issachar answered Deborah's call to war, and they did not content themselves with sending soldiers but took part in the war themselves. And as they supported her, they also supported Barak, her partner in declaring and leading the war, and showed him all loyalty, so they followed him in his going down to the plain, where they fought the battle under his leadership. As for Reuben, he let down his brothers, for he wasted time in discussions and deliberations, sitting by the streams of the rivers, over whether to go out to the war or not to go out, and it ended with a decision not to take part with his brothers in the war. And this deserves God's condemnation, spoken by Deborah.

5.15.0.en: Why abodest thou among the sheepfolds, to hear the bleatings of the flocks: why did you prefer to stay among the folds of your sheep and hear the whistling of the shepherds to their sheep to lead them to drink, instead of going out to the war. For the divisions of Reuben there were great searchings (inquiries) of heart: by the tributaries of the Jordan River in the land of Reuben the Reubenites sat deliberating whether they should go out to the war to help their brothers or not.

5.15.1.en: The tribe of Reuben preferred to stay beside the folds of its sheep, hearing the whistling of the shepherds to the sheep, rather than listening to the sound of the trumpet of battle. Therefore Deborah mocks them, describing their decisions, which sprang from their own thinking, as great decisions, in mockery and derision, for they were of course very wrong decisions, since they preferred laziness and slackness to sharing the war with their brothers.

5.16.0.en: Abode in his breaches (in his ports): the land of Asher was next to the sea, and he continued to dwell in its harbors without moving to take part in the war. Breaches = the plural of "farda", that is, harbor. (Farda: harbor.)

5.16.1.en: Gilead, that is, the sons of Manasseh who lived east of the Jordan, failed in their duty and chose to remain dwelling in their land and not take part in the war as their brothers, the sons of Machir the son of Manasseh, who lived west of the Jordan, took part. So also did the tribe of Dan, which was content to sit in its land next to the Mediterranean beside the ships and did not hasten to help its brothers who were fighting. And the position of Asher was like that of Dan, for it remained at rest in its portion of the land on the seacoast and in its harbors.

5.17.0.en: High places (heights): the plural of "rabiya", a raised place, and there were heights in the field of battle.

5.17.1.en: Deborah had already praised the tribe of Zebulun in her song, and here she adds to the praise of it as evidence of its sacrifices and its disregard of any hardships and its giving of itself as a ransom for its people and its devotion to them. And the tribe of Naphtali took part with it with the same zeal and work, and did not mind any hardships in climbing the high places of Mount Tabor in the field of battle and being exposed thereby to the arrows of the enemy encamped there, but they stormed all the places, giving themselves as a ransom for their brothers.

5.17.2.en: We see here Deborah's concern to praise those who took part in the war, for the leader must praise those who labored with him and encourage them, and reproach the slack to encourage them to take part the next times.

5.17.3.en: Take care to share your brothers' afflictions, and labor and give as for yourself, because you are a member with them in one body, which is the Church, and God sees your labor and rewards you for it, in addition to your brothers' love for you.

5.18.0.en: Taanach: a city five miles southeast of Megiddo, in the portion of Manasseh west of the Jordan River (Map 10). The waters of Megiddo: a branch of the river Kishon mentioned in (ch. 4:7). Some other pagan kings joined the king of Canaan and allied with him in his war against the children of Israel, so they came to the city of Taanach, where their armies attacked the Israelites, thinking that they would defeat the people of the Lord and obtain spoils and release the Israelite captives for a ransom of silver, but they were defeated and obtained neither captives nor silver.

5.19.1.en: God supported His people, for He made the stars of heaven support the children of Israel in their victory over their enemies, and they sent lightnings that troubled them and then thick clouds that covered the sky with a near-darkness, which increased the enemies' confusion. And the moon too may have had an effect on the river Kishon in increasing the tide and ebb, which helped the enemies to drown.

5.20.0.en: That ancient river (the river of events): the river Kishon, in which important events took place over the course of history.

5.20.1.en: A severe tide and ebb occurred in the river Kishon, and the flooding of the tide waters helped the enemies to drown. Then Deborah calls the fighters to trample their enemies with strength because God is with them.

5.21.2.en: Sisera's soldiers, in their flight before the armies of the children of Israel, were driving their horses hard, so the horses ran swiftly and their feet struck the ground hard. These represent the one who relies on his military strength and not on God: he is defeated and withdraws fleeing from the war, and the vanity of his strength appears.

5.22.0.en: Meroz: a city near the valley of Jezreel in Galilee, that is, the north of the land of the Jews, and it has now vanished from existence.

5.22.1.en: The people of the city of Meroz did not come to the help of the people of the Lord; they took a passive position when they saw Sisera fleeing, and did not seize him and hand him over to the people of the children of Israel as Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, did. It is a city that deserves a curse because they did not hasten to support the people of the Lord when they were fighting the mighty ones of Canaan, so the angel of the Lord curses them, that is, the one commissioned by God to help them in the war.

5.22.2.en: God loves you and is ready to support you in all your battles against the devil, and He moves the events of life, and even nature, to support you. So do not fear the harshness of the enemies, because your God is stronger than they, and persevere in your striving so that you may be victorious in the end.

5.23.0.en: In contrast to the curse that the city of Meroz deserves, Jael deserves every blessing above all women as a reward for the heroic courage she showed.

5.24.0.en: Deborah tells the details of what Jael did when she killed Sisera, and she added here a new detail not mentioned in the previous chapter, which is that she gave him butter to eat, not milk only, and presented it in an excellent bowl set aside for serving food to guests and the great men of the people.

5.25.1.en: The workmen's hammer: it is the mallet, that is, the hammer of the workmen, and it is so called because the workmen or laborers drive the nails with it when they pitch the tent.

5.25.2.en: Jael took hold of the nail in one hand and the hammer in her right hand and struck Sisera's head, so she crushed it and pierced his temple.

5.26.0.en: Sisera fell down from exhaustion, lying before Jael, who was standing before him in his service, and he had hardly taken the milk when he slept from the extremity of exhaustion, and in the place where he lay down to rest he fell dead.

5.27.0.en: When anxiety seized the mother of Sisera about her son, she began to look out of the window, crying out and asking why the return of his chariots was delayed.

5.28.0.en: The women attached to her heard her, and one of them answered her, one of her relatives or friends and the wisest and most experienced of them, and indeed the mother of Sisera herself answered her own questions, and her answer agreed with what her friend had said to her.

5.29.0.en: Their answers were an expression of what they hoped for of the victory of Sisera's army, which was only dreams that were not fulfilled, for they were expecting the following to be happening as an explanation of the delay:

5.29.1.en: Sisera's soldiers were dividing the spoils among themselves.

5.29.2.en: The portion of each soldier would be a girl or two whom he would take as maidservants.

5.29.3.en: Sisera's portion would be the finest garments made in the most beautiful colors.

5.29.4.en: And the portion of Sisera's mother would be garments embroidered with beautiful threads and cloths dyed in wonderful colors on both sides, some of which she would wrap around her neck to adorn it and increase her beauty; that is, she believed that the reason for his delay was the abundance of spoils he had taken and was dividing among the soldiers.

5.30.0.en: As Sisera and all his men perished, so the enemies of the Lord and the enemies of His people perish, while His beloved ones are exalted and their light shines, and all the darkness of the powers of darkness is dispelled before them, as the sun appears and all the clouds are dispelled before it.

5.30.1.en: As happens in every cycle, as we said earlier at the beginning of the third chapter, which begins with the people's disobedience, then discipline from the Lord, then deliverance, so it is here also: when the deliverance from the enemy was accomplished by the hand of Deborah and Barak, the people lived a period of stability and quiet lasting forty years.

5.30.2.en: Do not be occupied with daydreams like the mother of Sisera, but be a striver in the way of God and seek spiritual things and not material things, and you will be satisfied with the blessings of God.
